person.name: Alexander_Hamilton
person.summary: Alexander Hamilton rose from an impoverished childhood in the British Caribbean to become a Revolutionary War officer, constitutional advocate, and the first United States secretary of the treasury. He built federal financial institutions, helped define the Constitution's meaning, and became a leading Federalist before Aaron Burr mortally wounded him in a duel.

conclusion: The Federalist Papers remain a major source for judges, lawyers, scholars, and citizens interpreting the United States Constitution. Hamilton's public-credit system established federal debt management and regular customs revenue collection as central Treasury functions. The Bank of New York, which he helped found, continues as part of BNY Mellon.

events.date_note: Hamilton gave January 11 as his birthday. Sources differ on whether the birth year was 1755 or 1757
events.title: Birth on Nevis
events.description: Alexander Hamilton is born in Charlestown, Nevis, to Rachel Faucette and James A. Hamilton, who are not married. His household includes his older brother, James Jr., and Peter Lavien, his mother's son from an earlier marriage. James A. Hamilton comes from a Scottish family of minor landed gentry.

events.title: Loses His Mother
events.description: Rachel Faucette dies of [[yellow fever|yellow fever]] in Christiansted, Saint Croix, on February 19, 1768. Her death leaves Alexander Hamilton and his older brother, James Jr., orphaned. Johann Lavien, Rachel's first husband, seizes her estate.

yellow fever.explanation: Yellow fever is a viral illness spread by infected mosquitoes. Epidemics were a recurring danger in the Caribbean.

events.title: Leaves Saint Croix
events.description: Hugh Knox submits Hamilton's account of a devastating hurricane to the Royal Danish-American Gazette, a Saint Croix newspaper. Readers and community leaders collect money for Hamilton's education. In October 1772, Hamilton leaves Christiansted by ship for Boston and continues to New York City, where he boards with Hercules Mulligan before college.

locations.name_modern: New York City, New York, USA

events.background:
Before this opportunity, Hamilton had acquired unusual responsibility at Beekman and Cruger. The Saint Croix import-export firm had trusted him to run its operations for five months in 1771 while its owner was away at sea. He read widely outside work and had begun to look beyond the island.

The letter that drew attention had a religious and apocalyptic tone. It treated the hurricane as a divine rebuke to human vanity and pomposity. Ron Chernow wrote that its vigor was remarkable for a self-educated teenage clerk.

events.title: Defends the Patriot Cause
events.description: While studying at King's College in New York, Alexander Hamilton enters the public argument over resistance to British rule. He anonymously publishes A Full Vindication of the Measures of Congress and [[The Farmer Refuted]] in response to pamphlets by Samuel Seabury, a [[Loyalist|supporter of British rule]].

locations.name_modern: New York City, New York, United States

Loyalist.explanation: A Loyalist in the American colonies supported continued political ties to the British Crown during the conflict over independence.

The Farmer Refuted.explanation: Hamilton's longer 1775 reply continued his argument against Samuel Seabury's defense of British authority.

event_class.title: A Full Vindication of the Measures of Congress
event_class.impact: The essays establish Hamilton as a forceful young advocate for the revolutionary cause in New York.

events.title: Serves Washington's Army
events.description: In 1776, Hamilton raises and commands the New York Provincial Company of Artillery during fighting in New York and New Jersey. In 1777, George Washington appoints him an aide-de-camp on the Continental Army headquarters staff. Hamilton handles military correspondence and planning for Washington's army.

images.caption: Alexander Hamilton in New York Artillery uniform
images.creator: Alonzo Chappel

events.title: Marries Elizabeth Schuyler
events.description: Alexander Hamilton marries Elizabeth Schuyler at the Schuyler family home in Albany, New York, on December 14, 1780. Elizabeth is the daughter of Continental Army general Philip Schuyler and Catherine Van Rensselaer. The couple had met earlier that year in Morristown, New Jersey, while Elizabeth was staying with her aunt.

events.title: Takes Redoubt Ten
events.description: On October 14, 1781, Lieutenant Colonel Alexander Hamilton leads a Continental light-infantry column against British Redoubt No. 10 at Yorktown, Virginia. His troops take the fortified position with bayonets. The capture lets the American and French armies complete a second siege trench against Charles Cornwallis's forces.
events.background:
French naval control of Chesapeake Bay had sealed off Yorktown by sea. The French fleet brought heavy siege guns from the West Indies. Its victory over Sir Thomas Graves's relief fleet prevented British reinforcements from reaching Cornwallis. American and French forces then surrounded the British army and opened fire from their first siege trench.

Redoubts No. 9 and No. 10 were the last major outer defenses blocking a second trench closer to the British lines. Washington assigned Hamilton three battalions to work alongside the French assault force. The infantry were ordered to rely on bayonets so that an accidental shot would not expose the nighttime operation.

The French capture of Redoubt No. 9 and the American capture of Redoubt No. 10 gave the allies the ground for their second parallel. Allied artillery then moved closer and increased the bombardment. Cornwallis asked for surrender terms three days later. The British surrender ceremony took place on October 19.

events.title: Builds a New Career
events.description: In 1783, Hamilton returned to New York City and began practicing law in partnership with Richard Harison. He defended Tories and British subjects, arguing that New York law should be interpreted consistently with the Treaty of Paris.

locations.name_modern: New York City, New York, United States

images.caption: Bank of New York building at 1 Wall Street
images.creator: Jim in Times Square

events.title: Calls for a New Charter
events.description: In September 1786, Alexander Hamilton attended the Annapolis Convention in Annapolis, Maryland, with delegates from four other states to address trade barriers and the weakness of the Articles of Confederation. Hamilton wrote the convention’s final report, which urged Congress and the states to authorize a broader constitutional convention in Philadelphia.

Articles of Confederation.explanation: The Articles of Confederation were the first governing framework of the United States. They left most authority with the states and gave the national Congress no power to regulate interstate trade.

events.title: Writes The Federalist
events.description: In October 1787, Alexander Hamilton begins writing The Federalist Papers with James Madison and John Jay in New York City. Published under the shared name Publius, the essays argue for ratification of the proposed Constitution. They answer objections to its new [[federal system|federal system]].

locations.name_modern: New York City, New York, USA

images.caption: Title page of the first volume of The Federalist
images.creator: The original uploader was Anathema at German Wikipedia.

federal system.explanation: A federal system divides governing authority between a national government and constituent states. The essays defended the Constitution's plan to give the national government stronger powers than it had under the Articles of Confederation.

event_class.title: The Federalist Papers
event_class.impact: The essays help build support for ratification in New York and become a major guide to the Constitution's original structure.

events.background:
New York’s ratification debate faced strong opposition. The first essay appeared in the Independent Journal on October 27, 1787. Subsequent essays ran serially in New York newspapers through May 1788.

John Jay became ill after completing five essays. Hamilton supplied 51 of the 85 essays. Madison supplied 29. The essays were collected in two volumes in 1788. New York ratified the Constitution on July 26, 1788, by a vote of 30 to 27.

events.title: Becomes Treasury Secretary
events.description: On September 11, 1789, President George Washington appoints Alexander Hamilton as the first secretary of the Treasury in New York City. Hamilton takes charge of the new department. It collects federal revenue and works to establish the government's credit.

locations.name_modern: New York City, New York, United States

events.title: Funds the National Debt
events.description: In Philadelphia, Hamilton submits Report on Public Credit to Congress in January 1790. The report proposes that the federal government repay the national debt and take over the states' Revolutionary War debts. James Madison and Thomas Jefferson oppose the plan during Congress's debate.

images.caption: Hamilton’s 1790 Report on Public Credit
images.creator: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress

event_class.title: Report on Public Credit
event_class.impact: Congress adopts key parts of Hamilton's program, placing federal finances and public credit at the center of the new government.

events.background:
The new government inherited obligations to foreign lenders, domestic creditors, and the states from the Revolutionary War. Hamilton estimated the combined burden at about $79 million. Many federal certificates had changed hands after veterans and other original holders sold them at steep discounts. He urged payment at full face value to the current holders. He believed dependable payment would establish national credit and attach creditors' interests to the federal government.

State obligations formed the sharpest political dispute. The proposed federal assumption covered roughly $25 million in state debts. Representatives from states that had already paid much of their debt objected to sharing the cost. A private dinner arranged by Jefferson helped produce the Compromise of 1790. Madison agreed not to block the funding measures. Hamilton supported a permanent capital on the Potomac River. Congress enacted the funding and assumption measures later that year, placing the Revolutionary War debt under federal management.

events.title: Organizes the Federalists
events.description: In 1791, Alexander Hamilton founds the Federalist Party, a national political coalition supporting stronger federal power, public credit, and commercial development. Thomas Jefferson and James Madison organize the Democratic-Republican Party in opposition. The rival organizations form the country's first enduring national party competition.

events.title: Publishes the Reynolds Pamphlet
events.description: On August 25, 1797, Alexander Hamilton publishes [[Reynolds Pamphlet|the Reynolds Pamphlet]] after renewed accusations that his payments to James Reynolds involved [[Treasury speculation|Treasury speculation]] or public corruption. He admits his affair with Maria Reynolds. He says that James Reynolds had blackmailed him over the affair, and James Monroe, Frederick Muhlenberg, and Abraham Venable had gathered the allegations.

locations.name_modern: New York City, New York, United States

images.caption: Reynolds Pamphlet illustration associated with Hamilton
images.creator: gruntzooki

Treasury speculation.explanation: Treasury speculation meant using government financial information or influence for private gain. The accusation alleged that Hamilton had misused his public office.

Reynolds Pamphlet.explanation: The pamphlet's formal title was Observations on Certain Documents. Hamilton published it to answer allegations concerning payments to James Reynolds.

event_class.title: Observations on Certain Documents
event_class.impact: The pamphlet publicly confirms Hamilton's adultery while disputing allegations of financial misconduct in office.

events.title: Opposes Burr's Candidacy
events.description: In April 1804, Alexander Hamilton campaigns against Aaron Burr's bid for governor of New York. He shares severe criticisms of Burr's character with Federalist leaders. After a report of the remarks appears in print, Burr demands an explanation from Hamilton.

events.title: Dies After the Duel
events.description: Aaron Burr shoots Alexander Hamilton in a duel at Weehawken, New Jersey, on July 11, 1804. Hamilton is carried across the Hudson River in a delirious state to the Greenwich Village home of William Bayard Jr. He dies there from his wounds the following day.

locations.name_modern: New York City, New York, USA

events.background:
David Hosack treated Hamilton at William Bayard Jr.’s house. The bullet had damaged internal organs and lodged near his spine. Eliza Hamilton, their children, and close friends gathered during his final hours. Episcopal Bishop Benjamin Moore spoke with Hamilton about his faith and administered communion.

Hamilton’s funeral was held on July 14. Military companies and members of the Society of the Cincinnati joined a large procession. Gouverneur Morris delivered the eulogy at Trinity Church.

The encounter took place near the ground where Hamilton’s eldest son, Philip, had been fatally wounded in a duel three years earlier. Hamilton’s death weakened the Federalist Party. Burr was widely condemned for the shooting, and his political career ended.
